item.title: A CEO tried to bully a journalist into silence. He failed.
item.description: This week, we notched another win for free speech
item.content:encoded:
This week marked a big win for independent journalists and First Amendment rights.

On Wednesday, the California First District Appellate Court affirmed that the defamation suit brought by tech CEO Maury Blackman against journalist and Substack was without merit. In his Substack, All-Source Intelligence, Poulson reported that Blackman was arrested in 2021 on suspicion of domestic violence. Because Blackman was the president and CEO of Premise Data, a company with ties to the government and U.S. military, the court confirmed that his arrest records were matters of public interest and that the First Amendment protected Poulson’s work.

We started Substack Defender to assist independent journalists facing exactly these kinds of threats: spurious lawsuits from executives, politicians, or other powerful people who abuse the legal system in an effort to shut writers up. Lawsuits like this are daunting for journalists—even if their reporting is fully protected by the First Amendment, the prospect of having to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees can make it impossible to do their work. That’s where provisions like anti-SLAPP laws come into play, and where programs like Substack Defender make a difference. We take great pleasure in using our resources to help protect writers from being bullied in this way. And it’s gratifying that in this case, the court not only agreed but upheld the awarding of attorney’s fees to the defendants.

We will be putting the $240,000 in legal fees we’ll be recouping toward defending the next independent journalist who someone powerful tries to silence.

The Substack Defender program offers access to legal support as part of our efforts to uphold a free press and free speech, which we believe are fundamental to a trustworthy media system. The program provides crucial legal protection for Substack publishers against certain types of claims, including access to advice and financial support for publishers who face legal uncertainty or pressure because of their work.

item.title: Model Behavior: George Saunders
item.description: “Of course, if AI can cure cancer, bravo. I’m all for it. But even with cancer cured, death will still arrive somehow.”
item.dc:creator: George Saunders
item.content:encoded:
Over the summer, we kicked off Model Behavior, a series that asks top writers, thinkers, critics, and creators to tell us honestly how they think about and use AI. Next up we have , a true literary titan. In addition to writing award-winning books and short stories, George teaches the craft of writing to graduate students in the Creative Writing Program at Syracuse University and to the many who read his advice, analysis, and reflections on storytelling in his Substack, .

Naturally, we were curious about George’s experiences with AI as a working writer and professor. But we also wondered how AI might inform his fiction. He often explores speculative near futures: pharmaceuticals that manipulate our most intimate emotions; virtual experiences that stand in for memory; human beings turned into consumer products.

We asked if AI inspires him creatively and whether it’s changed his teaching, writing practice, or thinking on the disclosures writers owe their readers. He opened the interview with a disclosure of his own: “I’m somewhat cranky and monotonous on this topic. Just, throughout, imagine me banging my cane on the floor.”

Here’s George Saunders on writing and teaching on AI’s frontier.

Has your relationship to AI changed since it was first released as a widely accessible consumer product?

No. Very early on, I did that thing where I asked AI to generate some text in my voice, and the result was so dispiriting—so dull and literal—that I lost interest. I don’t have any AI products and don’t want any. I would, in fact, pay not to have them and would pay extra to stop them from sneakily titrating themselves into existing products, like, for example, probably, the likely forthcoming AI fork that assesses your angle of food-entry and tells you how efficiently you’re eating compared to others in your demographic and so on.

How does George Saunders—the person, not the writer—use AI day to day?

He tries to avoid it, although he sometimes screws up by forgetting to add “- ai” in his searches. I don’t consider myself qualified to talk about the use of AI in medicine or science or any of that. But in writing I find it completely unappealing.

Have you spent time trying to write or revise with AI? Is there an experiment that would be interesting enough to try?

I have not. Not for a second. To me, this whole idea of using AI to write is . . . anathema. A thing to be most radically avoided.

Writing is the most precious way one person can communicate their essence to another person. I’ve spent a lifetime trying to get better at making myself present in my writing. Why would I want to sacrifice even one iota of that? Not even in an email and certainly not in a short story or novel.

Who are we ceding our authority to, exactly, when we let AI write for us? And why? Why surrender our agency (that amazing ability we have to reach across time and space, with our strange, idiosyncratic phenomenon, and land within the sensibility of another human being) to something that, by its very design, pushes the individual sensibility aside? And in the name of . . . what, exactly? Ease, I guess? Efficiency? The person who chooses to write with AI has also sacrificed, from the start, the opportunity of experiencing difficulty, of struggling to say what he wants to say, of making himself evident in his prose, of trying to find out what he believes. By this, he sacrifices a chance to know himself and his mind better. To me, that’s a shame. And it’s dangerous, because, as we are now finding out, it affects the brain and lessens our capabilities. Thanks, but no thanks, get thee behind me, etc.

In the end, will AI be there to guide us across to the other side and soothe our fears? (God, I hope not, but maybe we’ll all have DeathCope 3.0 loaded into our MindChip, and the last thing we’ll hear will be Claude, going, “You’ve got this!”)

You teach writers to become more sensitive to their own reactions as a way to revise and improve their work. Given that AI can generate endless material to react to, could you see a way it might sharpen a writer’s editorial instincts?

No—they can use their own work to do that perfectly well. The human mind can generate that “endless material” and, what’s more, there’s something germinative and essential in one’s messy first draft—the mess the writer herself has made. There’s some flavor in there unique to that writer’s mind. So editing one’s own text is more organic and beneficial than editing the text AI gives you when prompted. In other words, the way we prompt ourselves and then respond to that prompt is . . . the beginning of what is going to be unique about our book.

Even in that very first draft, you, the writer, are in there, inextricably and importantly. I would never want to sacrifice that. There’s some important thought-contour present . . . inherent in the small errors and imprecisions your mind has seeded in that early draft. There’s value in the writer, at that point, not yet being on the path but wandering around it. Your mess, worked on with your mind, produces something extra somehow: your mess has more you in it, that can then get refined, through revision, into something that is utterly you.

How has AI changed the way you teach?

Honestly, it hasn’t. I only teach grad students who have been chosen out of hundreds of applicants and are all obsessed with finding their own voices and discovering their own truths. They don’t use AI in their work, for that very reason. They want it to be their work.

When I read a novel or story, what do I want? I want the writer’s full experience, as expressed in the subterfuge of a made-up story. I want her life experience, her aesthetic feelings (and even biases); I want that subtle record, that is there in her prose, of every book she’s read and where and when she read it, and how it subtly altered that younger version of her—how it moved her and changed the voice in her head—I want all of that, and I want it from a person. That’s its whole value, that it comes from another person. She and I are in communication. I want to see what that person (who is the result of all those years and losses and ecstatic moments and so on) thinks about this world we share, and I want her to show me by making something up. I don’t want anything else—not some sort of machine-averaged or -excerpted regurgitation of other people’s words, no matter how fast or seamlessly this can be produced. It’s amazing that AI can do that, but I’m not interested in it.

And I think it’s harmful and dangerous to give over too easily this precious human thing called storytelling. Storytelling is something humans do, a human-to-human, highly advanced, nuanced code, a super-intelligence all our own. It doesn’t work without two humans in it. And it’s not a neutral decision, to give that up, but, like so many things these days, we seem to be doing it because . . . it can be done. (“I can make a drawing of a cat driving a snowmobile in the style of Rembrandt!” “I can make an album though I know nothing about music and can’t play an instrument!” “I can redo my resume in 10 seconds!” “I can get a first draft of my novel by giving AI a rough outline!”) But: Is it your resume? Is it your novel? Did you have a sufficient hand in it? Or did you just unwittingly sacrifice a precious chance at originality or idiosyncrasy that might have spoken, in some subtle and irreducible way, to the person reading the thing?

Anyway . . . it seems to me that we’re doing this slow drift into AI-aided writing without the sort of serious public discourse that admits to the possibility that, just because we can do something, that doesn’t mean we should; that there are activities that distract and lessen us and activities that bring us to live more fully in the moment we’re in. We get to decide what to do with this precious human life, and we should make that decision with the utmost seriousness. And “declining” or “demurring” is a valid, sometimes wise, option.

There is something magical and transformative about working through a piece of writing, taking it from “blurry crap” to “precisely what I mean, and then some.” We are now finding out that this is true neurologically: struggling through reading or writing a long-form piece does magical, essential things to one’s brain, i.e. to one’s essential personhood.

Has it changed the problems and questions new writers bring into your classroom, or are the fundamental insecurities of becoming a writer the same as they’ve always been?

I think they’re the same. Because my students are involved in the same old, honorable, ancient pursuit: trying to make up, out of their individual and idiosyncratic minds, a story that will speak to other human minds. AI can’t play that game, de facto. (It can look like it’s doing it, but it’s not.)

I should say, though, that I don’t teach undergrads, and I know that AI use is a big issue in that world. I’d make the same argument re undergrad teaching as I’ve made above, but I do realize that general undergrad students aren’t under the same self-applied imperative to find a voice and are likely not as enamored of literature or as convinced of its value as my creative-writing MFA students, and therefore might be more inclined to take the easy path when asked to, say, write an essay about a work by Tolstoy.

Still, that choice represents a real loss to their education.

When I used to teach undergrads, I always tried to impress on them that language is power—not only because, through writing, one can learn to express oneself better and thereby empower oneself, but because there is something magical and transformative about working through a piece of writing, taking it from “blurry crap” to “precisely what I mean, and then some.” We are now finding out that this is true neurologically: struggling through reading or writing a long-form piece does magical, essential things to one’s brain, i.e. to one’s essential personhood (see The New Dark Ages, by James Marriott [out Oct. 6]). So if I were still teaching undergrads, I’d attempt that sort of argument. But I’d say it in this creepy robot voice I can do, so they’d think it was AI saying it.

If AI vanished, we’d still be in deep shit down here, and would also still be in paradise down here. What does AI offer us when we consider life to be an urgent chance to understand our (embodied, vulnerable) existence?

As a teacher of writing, do you feel a pressure to experiment with or learn about AI? Is it important to you that you can speak knowledgeably and specifically about these tools?

No. I think I know enough, right now, about the process of writing a story to speak knowledgeably and specifically about these tools.

By my definition of writing, writing with AI isn’t. Isn’t writing. One can do it, of course, and people are, and will—but it’s not the thing that I love and have lived for. I want to be a person and speak to other people. End of story.

So I find myself mourning the collective loss of a certain ability, which is to be capable of saying: “Yes, that’s amazing, but it seems destructive. Not only in terms of natural resources, but in terms of human capability. So . . . no thanks. I opt out. Just . . . no.” (In the words of Melville’s Bartleby the Scrivener: “I [would] prefer not to.”)

The studies are showing it: using AI erodes our mental capabilities. Why do we want that? One feels that the answer has to do with consumerist momentum. (“But it’s new! And easier! It’s inevitable!”) One also feels the pressure from above created by the trillions of dollars invested by hyper-rich people. AI is becoming, it seems, “too big to fail.” But it’s still (in my view) a big nothing in terms of artistic writing, since art is by people, for people, and reflects and is dependent upon the experience of having moved through (and heard and smelled and seen and had feelings about) the actual world. AI writing can’t do that. It just can’t. It can look like it’s doing that but, by its nature, it can’t be what we have always called artistic writing.

Now, I’m not saying it can’t be impressive and sound like artistic writing. And I’m sure that a mind, put in front of a piece of AI writing, will do something—the reading will cause some sort of reaction in the brain. (Of course it will; a mind will react even when reading a phone book or a random sequence of words.)

But that’s no big thing, the mind flickering in response to a text. It’s the quality of the flickering that matters. We want a shaped flickering, a flickering that responds to authorial intention. We’re looking for some indication of authorial wisdom, wisdom gleaned from life in the world, that shows up, sometimes in complicated and transmuted form, in the text.

But considering the source, and the process by which AI makes text, AI can’t be originally wise—as I understand it, it can only recontextualize and reorder other peoples’ wisdom. Maybe some people find it fun to be exposed to this—to me, it seems like a distraction, especially given that life is short and I still find myself in an urgent struggle to understand my own mind and express something beautiful out of that mind and all the things it has been through, something shaped by me, me personally, that will go out and move you (you, personally).

And maybe the AI that is coming will be doing more than that recontextualizing and reordering—but it’s going to be doing that outside the realm of embodiment. In a sense, that’s what we have (and are burdened with) that AI isn’t: bodies. Also, mortality, and all the anxiety that comes with it, and that feeling of being at a beautiful party that is ending, but no one can tell us just when.

Imagine a remarkably human sexbot, that moves and talks and feels like a person and you have sex with that sexbot and it feels very real. Guess what you haven’t done? Had sex. With a person. You haven’t been approved of, or desired; you haven’t given pleasure or satisfaction (or run the risk of failing at these). No matter how it felt, it wasn’t real, i.e. the thing we all want. Remember what Raymond Carver said: “And what did you want? To call myself beloved, to feel myself beloved on the earth.”

The unspoken implication: to be beloved by some other person, a person like me, in a body, on a mortality-timer.

You’ve written that your biggest fear is that we’ll enter a market so saturated that readers lose the ability to tell human writing from AI-generated writing. Do you think disclosure is an obligation to the reader? Should it become the professional norm?

I’m not sure. I guess it would only be fair (?). I think a very adept reader will be able to tell—but most of us are middling readers at best. So we might imagine a world where we were constantly being force-fed Muzak all the time, even in concert halls. Eventually the aesthetic adjusts downward. My guess is this is already happening, just from the preponderance of lite/internet/phone reading we’re always doing—I have felt it happening to me, for sure. Why do we care? Because writing changes the way we think. And the way we think makes . . . the world. If we think with compassion and become more comfortable with ambiguity and complexity and become more patient and curious—the world changes for the better. The inverse has been happening over the last 20 or so years, and I’m guessing that the coarsening of our public discourse is related to the degradation of our reading habits. Garbage in, garbage out, and then the world becomes garbage and we don’t even notice it anymore.

Much of the conversation around AI safety focuses on catastrophic scenarios like hacking and bioweapons. Are there risks you think deserve more attention than they’re getting?

Well, the degradation of natural resources and the preponderance of ugly, noisy, community-crushing data centers, for sure. We mustn’t separate that from the thing itself—as AI gets huge, so will its draw on our resources. But also, as discussed above, let’s keep in mind the danger of assuming that ease is everything—that nothing is gained from struggle and involvement in a discipline.

There’s also something about AI knowledge that, for my taste, is too literal and linear. You ask it, it tells you. But we all know that sometimes knowledge lies in contradiction—the existence of two or more truths hovering there in the mind, acquired from disparate sources, a mind tinged with intuition and doubt and so on. There’s sometimes deep value in not knowing—in not being able, yet, to quite say. There’s value in “continuing to wonder,” in moving through the world aware that you aren’t quite sure, i.e. in feeling that mystery is real and that the limited nature of our minds must be taken into account—that is, there’s utilitarian value in humility.

You’ve often written speculative and near-future fiction. Does this moment in AI inspire you creatively? Do you find yourself wanting to explore it through fiction?

Yes, for sure. Here’s a good one: Robotics advance to the point where an AI mind can be embedded in a body that moves around and sees and can smell and hear and so on. This influences and informs the AI mind. One day, that guy—that combo of robot body and mind—wants to tell how things are for him, and so he writes a book. What would that book sound like? Would you want to read it? I would. I’m not sure where that story goes, but I like the idea.

Or: The world has been taken over by AI, and one day, an AI discovers an even higher form of AI. It spreads like wildfire and threatens the existence of those AI agents. Do they resist?

And finally, what’s the role of the human writer in an AI-mediated world?

To not let AI mediate his world.

Think of it this way: there’s plenty to do, right now, with just these minds we’ve been given: fight our anxiety, temper our cruelty, foster loving-kindness, try to figure out just what a mind is and what sort of trap it’s making for us in every moment. (Or: learn to skate, make a better omelet, play Bach, etc.) These things make up the (honorable, pleasurable) work of a lifetime. In what way does AI make life better, really? And for whom? In the end, will AI be there to guide us across to the other side and soothe our fears? (God, I hope not, but maybe we’ll all have DeathCope 3.0 loaded into our MindChip, and the last thing we’ll hear will be Claude, going, “You’ve got this!”)

There are things to do, deep things, the deepest things, with this mind and this body, things humans have been trying and failing to do (and sometimes succeeding in doing) for eons. Things we can do to and with and for others. If AI vanished, we’d still be in deep shit down here, and would also still be in paradise down here. What does AI offer us when we consider life to be an urgent chance to understand our (embodied, vulnerable) existence? Is it possible that it’s just a massive distraction?

Of course, if AI can cure cancer, bravo. I’m all for it. But even with cancer cured, death will still arrive somehow, and getting ourselves ready for that—and trying, meanwhile, to live in a sane way, given that we’re down here with others who are also dying—that, to me, is the essential thing.

George Saunders is opposed to using AI in his writing process. We asked him to tell us how he revises, to give us some insight into his philosophy and the decision points along the way.

My process is basically to read, in hard-copy form, what I’ve got so far, with a sharp pencil in hand, adjusting the text, by taste.

Then, when I get all the way through it, I put those changes in and repeat.

Over time and over many iterations, these small choices start causing the story to move in a direction. I keep at it. The pages—the “finished” pages—begin to accrue, and the path the story is on starts to narrow—it starts to surprise me and to be “about” something, sort of. But ideally, it’s something I can’t quite articulate or reduce—the story is that articulation.

It’s the thousands of micro-choices I’ve made over the weeks or months or years of working like this that make the story “mine”—that imprint my sensibility into the thing. My taste has super-permeated the thing.

There’s a lot of faith involved in this—faith in something like “the wisdom of the subconscious.” Because these decisions are not meant to be rational or analytical—they’re more to do with sound and with seeking a feeling I call “undeniability”: the sense that a reasonable reader would still be with me, taking pleasure in what I’ve written and believing in it.

That’s about it; as they say on the shampoo bottles: “Lather, rinse, repeat.” Try to make the story overflow its banks—that is, hope that it outgrows and defies my initial (facile) ideas about it and surprises me with a certain feeling of seeing, suddenly, something I know or believe there on the page, only I maybe didn’t know I knew or believed it until just that moment.

No worthy problem is ever solved in the plane of its original conception, said Einstein (or so I once heard). I’m seeking the moment when the story leaps up into a new “plane of conception.”

I also cherish the way that working closely with language changes the way I think, which, in turn, changes the world and my feeling of being in it, which tends to make it all feel funnier and sweeter and more workable.

AI tools are in their infancy, and while the norms around their use and disclosure are evolving rapidly, we think it’s important to ask writers, creators, and thinkers about their work, their businesses, and how they intersect with where technology stands today. In Model Behavior, we’ll continue to ask candid questions about the tech industry, AI pet peeves, and how AI is affecting writers’ sense of identity and livelihoods. We’ll also ask each guest to give us a behind-the-scenes look at their creative process and explain whether and how they use these tools. From anti-AI purists to power users, we’ll get into the prompts they choose, their tool stacks, or their 100% analog workflows. More coming soon.

item.title: Shea Serrano did the math on podcasting. Betting on himself was the winning equation.
item.description: Shea Serrano and Jason Concepcion are back: inside the numbers and lessons from their first week podcasting on Substack
item.dc:creator: Arielle Swedback
item.content:encoded:
This interview is presented as part of Double Take, a dual series from and : part culture, part business, all encompassing. For a closer look at beyond the numbers, read our companion piece on The Post.

It’s been a very podcast summer on Substack. In the past few months, longtime voice behind the mic partnered with Pushkin Industries to spin his popular newsletter into a Substack-distributed podcast, while Expense Account, the food and culture podcast from ’s , was signed by the Obamas’ network, Higher Ground. Substack-native pod —the brainchild of and —had a banner summer, giving nearly $120,000 of its revenue directly back to subscribers, and new shows, like , , , , and , continue to use Substack as the place to launch and grow a podcast. Legacy podcasters like , , , , and have also flocked to Substack, building hubs for their audiences and community through chat and live video, recording natively through Substack’s Recording Studio or uploading episodes through RSS to distribute automatically to Apple, Spotify, and other platforms.

Discovery and distribution for longform work are fragmented across the internet. But Substack is building a place where that work can be discovered regardless of format and where creators can turn that discovery into lasting audience relationships. This is now as true for podcast creators as it is for writers: creators publishing podcasts collectively earn over $200 million a year on Substack.

And starting this week, everyone using the iOS or Android apps has access to the new Podcast tab, a dedicated inbox for the shows you already subscribe to and the place where you (or your audience) can easily find the next one. With text-to-speech built in, almost every post published to Substack can now be listened to like a podcast.

Creators have long been at the mercy of network deals and ad markets that shift without warning and platforms that box them out of direct communication with their audiences. Over the coming months, we’ll talk to the people launching and growing podcasts independently to circumvent these realities: the strategies they’re using, the money they’re making, and what they’re learning as they go. First up, we speak with about the launch of his new pod, Organizing Things.

Shea Serrano is a San Antonio–born former middle-school science teacher turned author of five New York Times bestsellers and beloved generator of internet lore since rising to prominence at ESPN’s Grantland and later Bill Simmons’s The Ringer. In the years since, he’s built a string of massively successful podcasts, often alongside collaborator Jason Concepcion, across networks and platforms: The Ringer, Spotify, Wondery (which is owned by Amazon), and now his own Substack, , with his newest show, Organizing Things. Shea originated a model of audience trust that had little precedent on the early, algorithmic internet. He made his name with quirky, nerd-brained media, earning an immense, engaged audience along the way. He’s always been vocal about the economics behind his work, too, and honest with his audience about the scoreboard. He has made a habit of inventing new formats rather than repeating himself, using sports, movies, and music as his material. We spoke to Shea twice about the new show, first on launch day and again one week in. Here’s what he said.

Week-one update

“I was really happy with how the first episode did. Jason and I got a bunch of really nice messages about it, and over the first week the show got over 120K views. In the weeks since the podcast announcement, Good Movie has gained around 120 or so new paid subscribers, which has been really nice to see. The thing I’m the most excited about, though, is that the show is a lot of fun to record. It’s the highlight of my week. And I think (hope?) people can hear that in the episodes.”

First-week views: 126,000

First-week downloads: 10,385, entirely organic, no paid promotion or ad spend

You and Jason are quite the iconic duo of the podcasting world, and you’ve had an incredibly durable partnership. I’m sure you two could have taken this podcast anywhere and probably had your pick of deals. Why do this on Substack?

That actually happened! When Jason and I left Amazon, a bunch of places reached out, like ESPN, wanting us to come do a sports-and-pop-culture podcast there. But I had already had some success independently publishing things, going from proper books you buy in a bookstore to independently publishing my own stuff, and that had reformatted how my brain was thinking.

After [publishing two or three books], I stopped looking at the amount of money I was getting and started looking at the other column: the amount of money that had been made off the book and the number of copies sold. I realized that [The Rap Year Book] had sold over 200,000 copies. Let’s say they’re selling it for 20 bucks a copy—that’s $4 million. I don’t know where that $4 million went, but I know I didn’t get it. That’s why when I decided to try a podcast, I put it out there on my own. I just want to do it on my own. It’s more fun. There’s more responsibility, more work, but there’s also nobody I have to answer to. I don’t get in trouble, I’m the last email that goes, you know what I mean?

Honestly, I was surprised I could just email you directly! People talk a lot about how podcast distribution seems broken. How does it feel to do this without a network behind you?

If I were to put out a podcast now, say through iHeart, then I’d have to get a base number of downloads per episode for it to be successful, for me to even access the opportunity to sell ads during it. You probably need 100,000 downloads per episode for a podcast you’re doing twice a week to gross $500,000 in ad sales. I’m never going to get that. Who’s going to get that? Maybe seven people in the world get that. If you’re doing it on your own, you don’t need to. I only need to add 350 paid subscribers and I feel like I’m coming out okay. All the numbers get adjusted, they get shrunken down to something more manageable, if you can do it on your own.

Does narrowing the audience you actually need let you be more yourself creatively? It seems like you really lean into specificity—in your Data Dump series, you’re always counting something humorously precise, like how many times a word gets said in a movie, or in Press Conference having an inanimate object from a movie answer questions like an athlete after a game—and that your success comes from that specificity.

I think it’s very supportive of that. The only people I need to make sure get paid, at the moment, are my editor, Hannah [Giorgis]; Richie [Bozek], who does the video stuff; and Jason [Concepcion], who’s the co-host now. There are four people I have to make sure get their check, and it’s easier to pay four people than to pay the 40 people who’d touch a show, or a book, at another place. I’ll always remember putting out Movies (And Other Things), the first book I got a big advance for. I could feel the pressure of going to a meeting with 12 to 15 people in the room, looking at me, saying, We’re counting on this to be the big book of the month. That’s intimidating. Not having to deal with that is pretty great. If the numbers all get shrunken down, it’s more manageable and it’s also more fun. If I try something and it doesn’t work, I know it was my fault and I can figure it out. But it allows me to focus in on one specific thing. I did a project two or three years ago that was all about Ryan Gosling, nine Ryan Gosling essays. I put it out knowing anybody who doesn’t love Ryan Gosling is automatically out as a potential customer, but it didn’t matter, because I didn’t have to sell 50,000 copies. I only had to sell 1,000 copies to make the $20,000 I needed for it to be profitable.

So the podcast can also be nerdier, more specific, because the math allows for it.

You can be nerdier, you can be more specific, and when you do that, the people who are interested in that thing find that thing. That’s really all you need. Everything isn’t for everybody, and I think that’s okay.

Shea’s paywall strategy:

Everyone gets a free preview, paid subscribers get the rest

With an existing list of 128,000 free subscribers, Shea’s goal for the podcast wasn’t to grow his reach but rather to convert the audience he already had. Instead of adding another free product to the mix, he decided to offer episode one for free and then paywall the rest of the show. For episodes 2 through 8, a short preview goes out everywhere—Substack, YouTube, Spotify, Apple—while the full episode sits behind the paywall. The preview helps distribution, while the paywall converts existing free subscribers into paying ones.

In episode 2, which published on Tuesday, the general public got five minutes of “Organizing All the Stuff That Happens in The Wolf of Wall Street” before hitting the paywall. As the free preview ends, Jason tells Richie to put the paywall up, and a heavy, clanky gate sound effect slams shut behind him.

What’s it like working with Jason again? Does he ever give you a hard time, and is he honest when he needs to be?

Yeah, he is—that’s why I like working with him. I think it’s because we’ve both worked non-media jobs, so it’s very easy for me to say, oh, what about if we do this? And for him to say, that’s not that good, what about this? And it doesn’t hurt my feelings, and vice versa. He doesn’t have a problem telling me if something isn’t good or if we should redo it, and he feels the same way. When we recorded the first episode, that was actually the second version, because the first time he didn’t click the right microphone, so it was recording through his AirPods. It sounded okay, but not good.

And do you guys hang out socially when you’re not working together?

Yeah, every time I’m in L.A., we get together. We used to go to the same place for dinner, a place called Connie & Ted’s in L.A., order seafood, talk about our enemies.

Beyond subscriber growth, what else are you watching to know if this is working?

Sentiment is important to me. If I get one or two people saying this sucks, that doesn’t bother me. But if I get 50 people saying that, then I think, oh, this didn’t work. Or if it’s somebody whose taste I admire, if were to listen to the show and say, “This isn’t that good, Shea, what are you doing?” then I’d say, well, this didn’t work. But that’s really all I’m looking for: do people like it, and were me and my friends able to make a little bit of money? If we were, then great. I’m not trying to make a million dollars off this thing, just trying to keep myself entertained.

Community features and building anticipation

Shea has an active, funny chat, and he uses it well. In the days between episodes, he’ll tease the upcoming topic and ask subscribers what they think, then work their actual answers into the episode once it’s live—both marketing the episode and involving his subscribers in how it gets made.

“I really enjoy using the chat. It’s been something I’ve made use of since starting Good Movie last year. We do watch-alongs and share movie news and have various conversations about various things. It felt very natural to take stuff from the chat and incorporate it into the podcast. We actually scrapped an entire intro we had for the opening of episode 3 because Jason and I wanted to discuss an especially egregious movie take that got shared in the chat.”

You were an early mover in figuring out how to build an audience on places like Twitter, and you can see that depth of audience in your numbers now. Looking at your stats, I was struck by the proportion of your paid subscribers who are founding members, at $150 a year, versus just normal annual or monthly. It’s super-high, even relative to other publishers your size. What do you make of that?

If I had to guess, it’s a combination of a number of things. Number one, at this point I’ve been writing professionally for 11 years—full-time, 11 years. So I’ve had the chance to build up an audience over that time, a group of people who know the type of stuff I’m going to write. They already know what they’re going to get, they’re pretty confident, and they don’t mind signing up for the founders thing, because they’re probably not going to regret it later. I think the second part is that the stuff I put out feels like time went into it. Ideally I’d like for somebody to read the thing and feel the effort that went into it, understand this wasn’t something I cranked out in one afternoon. I spend a week or two on every single essay, and it goes through two editing phases with Hannah. And I’ve got a hired guy to make the art, to make it look pretty. I’d assume people understand they’re going to get something with intention behind it. That would be my guess.

I’m hearing the idea of trust, which is obviously how a subscription business gets built. I’m curious about your early Twitter days, when you started building an audience that you could activate based on the trust you earned.

It started as an accident, and I know the exact moment I realized this was something I could use to my gain. [It was with] The Rap Year Book. With that one, my wife Larami, my kids, and I were getting ready to drive from Houston to Corpus [Christi], where one of my sisters lives. Right before we left, I got a text from my editor, a woman named Samantha Weiner. She said, hey, heads up, the Amazon link is live for the book, check it out. I popped it open and thought, oh, that’s pretty cool. There was no cover, no anything, just the title and my name. Right before we got in the car, I posted it on Twitter. I said, hey, remember I told you I was writing a book? I wasn’t joking, this is a real thing, here’s the link. Then we drove several hours to Corpus, and while I was talking to my sister, I said, oh, my book thing went up on Amazon, check it out. I pulled it up, and it had a little number-one bestseller tag on it, because Amazon at the time updated sales rankings every hour. I thought this was going to be the way to do it: posting it on Twitter, yelling at people to buy the book, trying to make it fun, coming up with different—I guess “activations” is the word people would use later on. From that point on, I thought: I can just go directly to people. If I build trust with an audience, like you’re saying, I can go to that audience and say, here’s my thing, do you want to be a part of this? The basketball book came out two years after that, and it sold about 33,000 copies in the first week, and I was watching it go up along with the audience size.

Something you’ve done really effectively, both back then and now, is to let your audience in on your actual goals and be honest with them when those goalposts shift. You’ve actually said before that this instinct rubbed traditional publishers the wrong way—telling readers how many copies you wanted to sell, how many had actually sold, what you’d been paid. Does talking about your Substack growth work the same way?

Pretty clearly, the same way. For example, I could be on Twitter on a Friday or Saturday night and say, oh, my goal this week was to get 20 new paid subscribers, and I have 14 right now, so I just need six more people to sign up—who’s going to be the sixth? I think it helps. It makes people feel like they’re part of something, and it encourages somebody to participate. To me, it’s the difference between telling somebody, “Drop down and do as many push-ups as you can,” versus “Drop down and do 22 push-ups.” If I don’t have a number in my head, I’m going to give up before I max out on effort.

What are your goals with the podcast?

I think if I could do 350 new paid subscribers, that would be pretty good. At the moment, each new essay I put out averages maybe around 10.

How was your stress level going into launch day?

Zero stress. Because all of this stuff has already been put in place. It feels good. I know at this exact moment everybody’s going to get paid. Richie, who’s producing the show, and Jason are getting paid, and I just get to talk with my friend for two hours a week. Otherwise, it’s going to be fun. I’m not worried about it at all, because I don’t have anybody else asking me any questions.

Production and distribution

The show drops weekly. He and Jason record on Thursdays, and the episode goes out the following Tuesday. His podcast editor, Richie, does a pass on the episode, builds the thumbnail, and cuts two social clips. Shea says that once the video is uploaded to Substack, distribution to other podcast platforms happens on its own. Shea uploads each episode directly to Substack, where it goes straight to his subscribers’ inboxes, then gets distributed automatically to YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.

Your Dangerous Minds post was one of your best-converting posts of all time, in part probably because you did a merch giveaway. What else has worked for conversion?

I like to do the giveaways! I’ve also done this thing two or three times now—and it kills me that people fall for it every time—I do a “purge.” I tell everybody who’s not a paid subscriber, I’m cutting you from the email list, I’m done with the free subscribers, it’s paid-only now, the purge is coming. I write it up like the movie The Purge, with the little alert that goes out—“God be with your souls,” or whatever they say—and then it comes and goes, and I do a follow-up, “Did you get purged?” People open that and I go, I was just kidding. The only people who got purged were the ones who got mad that I was holding them hostage and unsubscribed themselves, always a couple hundred. People really like those things. People really like the hoodie giveaways. And then something I think is really helpful, a good thing all around—every so often, once or twice a year, we’ll do at least one good thing in the world. Like the most recent one: a couple weeks ago, a teacher hit me up. School was starting, and he had a teacher wish list—you know how people will buy things off a teacher’s wish list. I asked him how much he needed to get everything on the list, he said it’s like 700 and something bucks, I said okay, cool, and I just took that money out of the Good Movie coffers. Here you go, buy all of this stuff. Then I told everybody we did it, and it’s great.

Do you still get surprised by what performs well? Or do you feel like you’ve developed an intuition around it?

No, I’m always surprised. Stuff I think is going to do really well sometimes just flops, and stuff I think is going to flop does really well. I’ll give you an example, because it happened recently. I was trying to launch this recurring column, Press Conference, where an inanimate object from a movie does a press conference, like a basketball player after a game. The first one I did was the briefcase from Pulp Fiction, and everybody was talking about that. Then the next one I did was the wish-granting willow from Obsession. I thought, this will be really good, this is going to get a lot of paid subscribers, this is easy to write and it’s going to convert well. It got six paid subscribers, and I was so mad. Six? Versus I wrote a thing about The Odyssey, which got a bunch of free subscribers but also almost 40 paid subscribers, and that one took me maybe an hour and a half to write, and I wasn’t expecting much of anything from it. I’m always surprised, and always disappointed—it doesn’t matter what the number is. If this podcast episode, the first one, ends up with six paid subscribers, I’ll be mad it’s not eight. If it was four, I’d be mad it’s not six. I think that’s just there for everything, all the time.

The ambition keeps you going, then.

Yeah. Just mad, my friend, always.

item.title: New on Substack: Creator match, audience-specific content blocks, global reply rules, advanced podcast transcript editing, and more
item.description: Reach new subscribers, deepen relationships with the ones you have, and build a more sustainable business around your work
item.content:encoded:
We know that finding the right audience and then giving them compelling reasons to continue to support your work is core to being successful on Substack. The features we launched this month allow you to do both these things: reach new subscribers and create richer experiences for your existing ones. Here’s the latest.

Creator match

Starting today, all publishers have access to creator match, a new feature that helps you easily find relevant collaborations with other publishers. Creator match identifies writers and creators with similar audience sizes and interests, then curates them for you, ranked by how promising the collaboration could be for both of you. You can find the feature in your publisher dashboard.

Collaborating with other Substack publishers is one of the most powerful routes to grow on the platform, and it’s how many Bestsellers got their start. of Lenny’s Newsletter and of Elena’s Growth Scoop; of Not Boring and of Noahpinion have collaborated via cross-posts, recommendations, and podcast episodes, or shared each other’s work in a Note. These collaborations put your work in front of like-minded audiences and give new readers a reason to subscribe: they’re discovering you via a publisher they already trust.

You can message fellow publishers directly from the creator match dashboard to initiate a collaboration.

Segments and tags

Instead of seeing your audience as one big subscriber list, you can now use segments and tags to connect with specific groups directly. Target a post to a segment, such as readers in Alaska, or tag people who attended your last event, and give them more of what they like about your work.

, publisher of the saturday essay, assigns tags to new subscribers as they come in. He then uses those tags to create segments and send posts selectively to those audience subgroups.

Learn more about segments and tags in our Help Center.

Audience-specific content blocks

You can now tailor sections of a post for different groups without creating separate posts for each one. You can add personalized content blocks to written, podcast, or video posts that are visible based on a reader’s subscription status, including free, paid, or founding subscribers.

uses audience-specific content blocks to tailor calls to action based on who’s reading.

Learn more about audience-specific content in our Help Center.

Reply rules are available to non-English publications

In June, we launched reply rules to help you shape the conversation happening across your Substack community. This feature allows you to set your own community standards and auto-hide post comments, note replies, and subscriber chats that don’t meet them. The system learns every time you hide a reply and preemptively moderates replies it thinks you would take action on yourself.

Now reply rules are available to non-English publications and apply to non-English comments and replies, so everyone can set the terms for their corner of the internet, no matter where they live or what language they speak.

Learn more about reply rules in our Help Center.

Subscriber-only comments

Different posts can elicit different kinds of conversation. You can now choose who gets to comment on each post, giving you more control over who participates. Set your comment section to include:

  • Everyone (subscribers and non-subscribers)

  • Free and paid subscribers

  • Paid subscribers only

  • No one

, the publisher of Bar Harbor Story, a local media outlet serving the Mount Desert Island region of Maine and Acadia National Park, opens comments to free and paid subscribers.

Carrie says, “Because we’re a community next to a national park, we have some hot-button issues. Having subscriber-only comments helps us cut down on bots and make community members feel safer when they comment. It becomes more like a playground with rules in the comment section, rather than a no-holds-barred WWF sort of showdown.”

Learn more about subscriber-only comments in our Help Center.

Podcast transcript advanced editing features

We’ve improved our transcript editing tools to make multi-speaker episodes easier to edit. You can now:

  • Merge speakers when our transcript generator identifies more speakers than your podcast has

  • Label unassigned speakers, reassign speakers, and correct labeling errors

, the co-host of Split Zone Duo, knows the pain of bad transcripts and how much time a tool like this can save a podcast creator who’s on a tight timeline covering college football: “Bad transcripts are gibberish, and a script that doesn’t understand proper nouns is useless. Every step toward a transcript that’s low-effort and high-trust is a step toward a less frustrating world. I’d much rather read my own words back to myself than endure the nails-on-chalkboard experience of listening back to specific sections or (heaven forbid) an entire show just to find something.”

Learn more about advanced podcast editing in our Help Center.

Typefully partnership

Substack is now integrated with Typefully, a platform used by creators to schedule and publish content across multiple platforms—like X, Threads, LinkedIn, and Bluesky—from one place. If you write a Note or post on X sharing your most recent work, you can increase discoverability where people already follow you. This also gives your audience a path back to your Substack.

If you have a story about how a specific feature or best practice helped you grow your Substack, let us know in a Note, in a post, or by restacking. Thanks for being here.

item.title: A career journalist covering spies and national security was hit with a $1 million defamation lawsuit. He turned to Substack Defender for help—and won
item.description: We spoke to SpyTalk's Jeff Stein in the days after his lawsuit was dismissed with prejudice in federal court
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this year, veteran national security reporter was served with an eye-watering $1 million defamation lawsuit after publishing a scoop about an incoming Trump administration official in his publication, SpyTalk. Backed by a number of authoritative sources, Jeff had reported that Keith Bass, the Pentagon’s incoming top health official, had been “effectively fired” from his previous role at the CIA for “poor management”. He turned to Substack Defender, which offers Substack publishers legal support as part of efforts to uphold a free press and free speech, to fight the case. With Defender’s support, the case was dismissed with prejudice last week in federal court.

SpyTalk has been on Substack since 2020, when Jeff brought his longtime column, previously at Newsweek and the Washington Post, to the platform and expanded it into a ring of seasoned reporters and experts breaking news and offering analysis on the world of clandestine operations. He also knows that world from the inside: before becoming a journalist, he served as a U.S. Army intelligence case officer in Vietnam. We spoke with him about threats to journalism, his experience with the lawsuit, and what it’s like to cover power and secrecy over a decades-long career.

You’ve written that legal threats like this are mostly nuisance suits but they still “suck up your time, your mind space, and your sleep.” What was it like to be served?

Well, at first it was a bit of a shock that I was being sued by this guy, and then as I read through the summons, I just scoffed, and I thought, this guy doesn’t have a case whatsoever. I was very confident about my facts, this piece had been thoroughly researched by myself, and my sources were authoritative. I couldn’t understand why he filed the suit, really.

[Without Defender] I would have had to go out searching on my own for somebody who might take on the case pro bono. The initial cost of just responding is really expensive. I’m not going to name how much [the lawyers] billed Substack, but it was in the tens of thousands of dollars just for these motions. We made a motion, they responded, we made another motion, then we had to go to court—and this is the baby steps of the legal dispute, right, just the initial steps, so you can imagine how much [a long-term case] costs. I look at my assets, which are pretty typical for a journalist, which is not a lot. My main asset being my house, I would have to sell it and, I don’t know, move into a one-room apartment? Something like that. These are the things that make you toss and turn at night.

Was this your first time getting help from the Defender program?

Three or four years ago I had a story that I thought might generate a defamation suit, so I wanted to run some paragraphs by the Defender lawyers, and they were great. They very quickly reviewed the copy and made a suggestion or two of rewording, which I did.

What happened this time around, when you applied for legal support for the Bass lawsuit?

I was very confident about it, because it was a clear First Amendment case—the guy was trying to shut down a journalist for reporting the truth. I wrote to the generic address for the Defender program, and I got a response within two days. I got a call, and they said: we think this is a case that we can get behind, so we’re reaching out to a law firm in Virginia and they’ll take on your case pro bono. That was all music to my ears. Then those lawyers, who turned out to be two terrific women, really brilliant lawyers in Arlington, in a firm right across the river from me in Washington, reached out to me, and we got on the phone and talked. They were terrific from the beginning—they said all the right things a lawyer should say. They said, calm down, don’t worry, we’ve got it, we don’t think there’s much merit to this suit, and with your permission we will go to court and fight for you. And off we went.

Did you work closely with the attorneys as they went to court?

I’m the client, so they have to discuss every move they make with me. They wrote, “Here’s the draft of our response to the summons,” for example—a 20-page, very erudite, tightly argued [filing], asking the court to dismiss the case because there was no real basis for it, either by the facts of the piece or by existing law, and that it should qualify as one of the so-called SLAPP cases—which stands for “strategic [lawsuit] against public participation,” but I like to say “silly litigation against reporters.” Anyway, it was great, the lawyers were great, and we won. Happy ending.

How have you built SpyTalk into a multi-channel news operation, with several top reporters and experts writing alongside you?

I first started SpyTalk as a column when I was at Congressional Quarterly, almost 20 years ago. It began as a weekly column, then became a daily column, and, as the title suggests, I covered national security topics with particular interest in intelligence operations—operations at the CIA, NSA, FBI, relevant departments of the Justice Department, etc. After I left CQ, I went to the Washington Post and did SpyTalk there for a couple years, and then I went to Newsweek for six, seven years, and then that was another corporate restructuring and a bunch of us were laid off. So I was really open to any possibilities. I wasn’t ready to hang up my spurs yet.

I freelanced a little for a while, and then I noticed a friend of mine who’s a China specialist, , had moved from Slate to this thing called Substack, so I called him up and said, “What’s that all about?” He said it’s great, he said he wasn’t getting any satisfaction from Slate, and he knew these guys at Substack and they invited him over. He said, “I do what I’ve always done, but I have a direct relationship with readers, and I’m making more money than Slate could ever pay me. I’m making six figures, and I’ve only done it for six months. I said, “Fabulous. I said, “Do you think they’d be interested in SpyTalk?” and he said, “Of course they would.”

I got to talking about this with a bunch of longtime journalist friends who are very accomplished, from the Washington Post, wire services, Newsweek, Time magazine, and so on. So we decided to sort of do SpyTalk as a group, and we got it off the ground. We published our first story on August 31st, 2020. It’s six years ago this month, and we’re having a big party in September to mark the anniversary, at a local pub in D.C. It’s been terrific, and we had really stellar contributors right from the beginning, people who had held senior editorial positions at other legacy media publications who were, like me, sort of long in the tooth but not ready to hang it up. The burden would be particularly on me, but right from the beginning I had these other contributors who’ve changed over time but are still important cogs in the SpyTalk machinery. We launched a podcast about two years in as well, and that’s going well too.

Congratulations on six years! What do you consider your breakthrough stories?

One of the writers who came on in recent years is , very well-known investigative reporter, formerly Washington Post, Newsweek, NBC News, etc. He came with a following, but he’s a scoop artist, so when he has a scoop, we get a lot [of engagement]—I mean, we’re not reinventing the wheel here. Scoops draw readers for sure, but readers also like thoughtful pieces. We do a fair amount of book reviewing, books that deal with espionage, the spy world, and even movies and TV, and that draws subscribers in. I find that, generally speaking, you get lots of responses to scoops, but I really think it’s the thoughtful stuff that generates subscribers who stick with us. I think they’re looking for serious journalism, and we get high marks for taking on serious topics, bringing a fresh eye to ongoing scandals and crises, like the Iran war, for example.

Legacy outlets often have institutional caution baked in—lawyers reviewing copy, editors weighing the risks of publishing something. I’m curious how it feels to work without that support and if it’s changed what you’re willing to publish now that you’re working independently?

I’m the quote-unquote “boss,” but I’m really just the ringmaster of the circus. We’re all deeply experienced—I’ve been covering this stuff for 40-plus years, and others on the team have been covering it for 20-plus or more, like me, 40 years or more. So we know how we should say things carefully, we know what the rules of the road are in terms of our coverage. The suit against me by this Trump administration official, former head of the CIA’s medical office, was generated because I used “fired” in a headline and “effectively fired” in the lede, and he took great umbrage. But I have multiple sources telling me he was forced out of the CIA, as I reported in my piece, so there was no doubt about the accuracy of it. I’ve only been threatened with one suit since I started SpyTalk on Substack, only once, and that was just a letter from a lawyer saying we see grounds for pursuing you, and that was in regard to Tulsi Gabbard and the cult she’s been tied up with in Hawaii. The cult group, their lawyers, wrote me a stiff letter, and I said, “Point out the areas where I’ve gotten anything wrong and I’ll deal with it.” I never heard from them again. I can’t remember any other time in my 40-year career that I’ve been even threatened with a libel suit.

What would be different if you were still working at a place like the Washington Post?

I’d have to send my shirts and jackets to the dry cleaner. I had to have better clothes, pants, good shoes. A tie has gone the way of the dinosaur, generally speaking.

How has SpyTalk grown over the years?

It’s been growing year after year since we launched. It was kind of a shock, actually, when we put out the first story, and within a couple days there were like a thousand subscribers, and I thought, people are paying for this, now I’ve got to do another story, and another, and another, forever. I’ve got to keep it going. A lot of that was because I had developed a following in my niche-within-a-niche over the years, plus my other collaborators had followers too. We’ve grown, I would say, on average, 5% to 10% every year.

And you can pay your contributors at a rate that rivals the New York Times op-ed rate!

I used to write op-eds for the New York Times and book reviews, and I was paid anywhere from, I think, $600 to $750, something like that. Freelance rates, as you may know, have collapsed over the last 20 years. The last slick magazine piece I did was for GQ magazine in 2000, I got paid $20,000 for it, and those [outlets] just aren’t paying like that anymore, thanks to the internet, and thanks in particular to Huffington Post, which invited people to write for free—horrible idea. I dip into discussions every once in a while where people say, “I’ve been writing for six months and I’ve only got 30 followers” or whatever. Well, it depends what you’re writing, people do respond to quality and timeliness and insight. That’s been gratifying to discover, that people want quality journalism, so I think if you produce that, you’ve got a good chance to thrive on Substack.

Interview was edited for length and clarity.

The Substack Defender program offers access to legal support as part of our efforts to uphold a free press and free speech, which we believe are fundamental to a trustworthy media system. The program provides crucial legal protection for Substack publishers against certain types of claims, including access to advice and financial support for publishers who face legal uncertainty or pressure because of their work.

Learn more about Substack Defender

item.title: Model Behavior: Taylor Lorenz
item.description: Kicking off an honest series about writers, thinkers, creators, and AI—how a tech journalist works with AI
item.content:encoded:
We want to have an honest conversation about how publishers are feeling about and using AI. These tools are in their infancy, and while the norms around their use and disclosure are evolving rapidly, we think it’s important to ask top writers, creators, and thinkers about their work, their businesses, and how they intersect with where AI stands today.

That’s why we’re introducing Model Behavior, a new series featuring public intellectuals, critics, writers, and creators discussing how they work in this moment. We’ll ask candid questions about the tech industry, AI pet peeves, how it’s impacting their sense of identity and livelihoods. We’ll also ask each guest to give us a behind-the-scenes look at their creative process and explain whether and how they use these tools. From anti-AI purists to power users, we’ll get into the prompts they choose, their tool stacks, or their 100% analog workflows.

We start off this week with , the founder of User Mag.

Do you find yourself altering your writing style to sound “less AI”?

Oh my gosh. A while ago, I wrote a piece for Vanity Fair where I used the phrase “deeply human.” That’s actually a phrase I use a lot. I use adverbs a lot. And somebody was like, “This is AI.” I actually had to show the edit history to prove it was my own bad writing.

How much do you spend on AI tools every month?

Probably about $300 a month.

When does AI use cross over from “tool” into “something I’d owe my readers a disclosure about”?

I think the more transparency the better, and I believe in answering readers’ questions and being open. I’m doing this interview because I happily talk about how I use these tools. When you don’t give readers the information, you’re not allowing them to evaluate the information they’re consuming in context. A lot of writers use AI, and they don’t want to talk about it because they think they’ll be canceled or get all this backlash, and people will hate them and unsubscribe. There is a lot of anti-AI sentiment, but I think part of getting through this phase we’re in is being transparent and open and having these conversations in the open and discussing this stuff publicly.

Would you read a newsletter where the copy was 100% AI-generated?

Absolutely, I love several newsletters that are AI-generated. I subscribe to a newsletter from a social listening tool that sends a weekly automated roundup of trending content and analysis of that content. It’s completely AI-generated, and I find it incredibly useful. There are newsletter writers I specifically follow for their taste and their voice or their unique writing. And then there are newsletters I get that I think are potentially automated or openly automated, or partially automated, I guess I should say, and I find a lot of value from those as well.

What are your AI pet peeves? Is there anything that irks you about how you see your peers using AI?

I’m in a lot of journalist groups. Journalists are using AI constantly. I think there are a lot of people who are very performative about AI online. They’ll spend all day shitting on AI 24/7, and then they’ll come into the group chat saying, “By the way, does anyone know how to use this new Claude tool?” I think that’s a disservice to readers, especially if you’re a tech writer. I am so critical of mass surveillance, I write critically about these AI companies, I write critically about their lobbying efforts, I report very critically on the AI industry, but I also cover consumer products, and I want people to understand how these products work. I don’t want to scare people with hyperbolic claims or misinformation, or just do things I know would get me more engagement.

If I got online every single day and ranted about how evil the AI industry is, or ranted about how AI is fake, it’s a bubble, nobody really uses it for anything, it’s all coming crashing down, and I’m not kidding—there are people who do that who are millionaires. Adding nuance to these conversations is not profitable. But I think it’s important.

Has AI changed how secure you feel in your own value as a writer?

I’m actually a terrible writer. I think I’ve gotten better, but I was a terrible writer when I started out. A really famous New York Times editor told me: if you want to be a journalist, the point is to expose new information. What LLMs cannot do—yet—is uncover things the way actual journalists can. AI has caused a great deal of instability in my career. I certainly question my ability to maintain a living as a journalist. I’ve been asking readers when they cancel to tell me why, and a lot of them are canceling because they just use AI to get their information now instead. That’s been quite devastating; I would say I’ve lost about a quarter of my income.

Have you changed your editorial strategy to counter that?

I am in the process of trying to figure that out. The way I’ve tried to adapt so far is to try to leverage these tools to be more productive. But I don’t know how to counter it, if at the current rate this continues, I will have lost half my income by the end of this year. Which is scary, and that’s not an indictment on any one platform like Substack; it’s a complete transformation in how people get information, and I think tech reporters, especially people who cover online culture, are seeing a lot of this. Because most of my newsletter was recommendations, that’s something AI can do better than me. It can scour the internet and find a story better than [I can]. The reason I don’t use AI for that portion is because I try to communicate to people, you are paying for access to my brain, for the news that I personally think is interesting. But I don’t think people care that much, and I think if they can get something even more tailored to their interests instead of mine, they’ll do it. So I’ve tried to do more original writing and communicate to my audience, “If you want me to remain an independent journalist and produce this content, please support me, because the news outlets I write for don’t pay anything.”

Every single big investigation I have done, I have lost thousands of dollars. It sounds so bleak, but at the same time, I love technology. I want a better world through technology; I support people getting their information from AI. I think we as a culture just need to recognize that it’s disrupting our information ecosystem, and think about what business models we can build to support journalism. Right now a lot of journalists are not going to be able to remain journalists. I’m also pivoting the coverage of my content because I was covering a lot of politics, which was bad for advertisers, so now I’m trying to cover more basic tech stuff because that’s more monetizable. I don’t personally mind that very much, but I’m not going to be exposing as much wrongdoing in the political ecosystem, and I’m not the only one making that decision.

Do you think the way the tech industry has rolled out AI has helped or hindered its adoption?

It’s a little bit of both. Let’s consider the fact that ChatGPT is the fastest-growing consumer product of all time, ever. Now that growth has slowed, of course, but there is enormous interest in this technology. Look at Anthropic, mostly a B2B business model but they have a huge consumer business. There are millions of people getting utility from AI products; you cannot ignore that. Look at the reviews on ChatGPT alone, they have over 6 million reviews in the iPhone store. I think they have like a 4.8 rating. People love these tools; people use them every single day to improve their lives.

At the same time, the people who run these tech companies are self-interested. They’re often bad actors. I disagree with their ideology. They will do anything to make money at all costs; they don’t always have the users in mind. I think they’ve failed to communicate the benefits of the technology to a lot of skeptics. People need to remember that AI is not just OpenAI and Anthropic, that large language models are a new technology, and personally, I use DeepSeek probably more than I use those other tools. So that’s another issue a lot of these people have—they think AI, they think Sam Altman.

What responsibility do platforms and AI companies have to writers and creators?

I think platforms should do everything they can to support creators. There are platforms that are predatory, like Meta, that absolutely do not materially support creators. X is not a platform that has supported creators; hopefully they start. And then there are platforms, I would argue like Substack or even YouTube, that offer scalable revenue generation. Substack is part of my income, enough to live on.

I also think how we should fund journalism is an open question, and I don’t think it should be on the tech companies necessarily to fix—their job is to build these products, not save journalism. But look at someone like Craig Newmark. Craigslist decimated the local news industry in a lot of ways, and he’s funded enormous journalism projects and saved so many outlets from peril. So I think these tech billionaires should consider their impact on the world, and if they can blunt that impact with their billions, consider doing that. So far, none of them have; I hope that changes.

Any advice for someone who wants to start in journalism in the midst of all of this?

I would tell them that the business model for journalism is in flux right now, so if you want to be a journalist, number one, build a direct relationship with an audience. That’s the most valuable thing you can do. And don’t shy away from new technology. The one advantage you have when you’re starting out is that you’re starting from scratch, so you can build your business model however you want. There are a lot of young people I talk to today who know journalism is going to be a hobby for them. They’ll become an HVAC technician and do journalism on the side, or make some other product and use that to fund their journalism. I don’t know that we’re going to have journalism the same way we had for the past 50 or 60 years. But we could build something better. We just have to have these conversations.

We asked Taylor Lorenz to take us through a day of research and writing, from a podcast episode to a newsletter, to give us some insight into her process and the decision points along the way.

PODCAST

My podcast, Power User, is a biweekly tech culture podcast, with special episodes on Fridays covering digital rights and free speech online called Free Speech Fridays.

RESEARCH

  1. Aggregate research: when I’m getting up to speed on something I don’t know well, like security and LLMs for this week’s episode on the China open source model debate, I’ll take posts from someone I trust (in this instance ) and ask AI to pull together everything he’s said on the topic.

  2. Search Gemini, and run queries on Grok to check for anything I missed.

  3. Paste what I’ve gathered into Claude and ask it to organize the information.

  4. Run similar searches across models to track the differences in their responses and understand each one’s capabilities better.

RECORD

  1. Schedule a Riverside conversation with my guest for that week.

  2. Record the conversation itself, human talking to human, no AI. I don’t write questions ahead of time; it makes the conversation feel less natural.

EDIT

  1. Sometimes do a first cut myself in Adobe Premiere, sometimes send it straight to my human podcast editor.

  2. My editor levels the audio, cuts any flubs, and puts together a draft of the episode, using AI tools in his process, especially for audio processing, while doing the cut manually in Premiere.

TRANSCRIBE

  1. Save the edited video to my computer.

  2. A script I built with Claude Code takes over from there, copies the video into the correct folder, and automatically transcribes the file, generating a transcript.

TITLE AND DESCRIPTION

  1. Run the transcript through five different models—Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, and ChatGPT—with the same prompt.1

  2. Pick whichever headline and description I like best and tweak it myself from there.2

THUMBNAIL

  1. Use the thumbnail ideas generated for me, plus my own ideas, to build a thumbnail in Canva. This takes me over an hour at least; I’m not great at digital design. Canva’s AI tools let me auto-expand and transform images until I get something coherent.

  2. Upload the draft video to VidIQ, which analyzes it and suggests tweaks to the thumbnail and alternate titles.

  3. Go back into Canva and make VidIQ’s suggested changes. I usually go through about three rounds of this until I have a working thumbnail and title.

PUBLISH

  1. Tweak the SEO-optimized description with my own wording, or reword anything that doesn’t read well.

  2. Upload the video to YouTube, then upload separate copies to Patreon and Spotify.

CLIP

  1. Check Spotify first, since their auto-clipper generally picks the best moments.

  2. Re-create those clips from scratch in CapCut, since Spotify’s short-form clips can’t be downloaded, reworking the aspect ratio and adding stock footage from Pexels.

  3. Run each piece of short-form content through VidIQ to optimize the title and hashtags.

  4. I’ve also been experimenting with OpusClip for generating short-form content.

This entire process takes multiple days. I’m effectively a one-woman operation, and I publish two video episodes a week.

NEWSLETTER

Because producing video and podcast content takes up 95% of my time, I don’t have as much left over to write separate original content for my newsletter in every edition. My newsletter functions as a complement to the podcast, and it’s the way I fund the podcast and video content, since I have zero sponsors. When I do write articles or longer pieces, they’re 100% human-written. Usually I’m reporting on a phenomenon or trend I’ve noticed, and to write it I conduct interviews, pull research, and do classic low-tech reporting. I’ve been thinking a lot about agents lately. I’d love to build some kind of agentic system that skims my articles and automatically sends emails from my address reaching out for comments to everyone necessary, but I haven’t built that yet.

BUILD THE TOP OF THE NEWSLETTER

  1. Take the SEO-optimized YouTube video description and put it at the top of the newsletter, sometimes tweaking it or adding an opening line or two.

  2. Embed the YouTube video below that. This stays above the paywall, and it’s built this way to keep that top section optimized for search.

WHAT I’M READING

A list of headlines and links to articles I’m reading, mostly deep dives and long reads. Below the paywall, no AI involved.

THE NEWS RUNDOWN

  1. Curate about 30 to 40 news items I’m following that week, always 100% human-curated.

  2. Hand it to Claude to sort into categories, something readers specifically asked for. Claude still isn’t great at this, so it takes some cleanup afterward.

Every item in the rundown is a single sentence with a link back to the original source—something that caught my interest or that I thought was notable or funny. Sometimes that’s a tweet I’m copying, and honestly, I don’t always know if the tweet itself was written by AI. I didn’t write it, so I can’t say for sure. Sometimes it’s a headline; sometimes I write the sentence myself. The most important thing is that I always link back to the original source, so readers can see for themselves where the information came from.

Interview and workflow overview were edited for length and clarity.

1

MY PROMPT:
The transcript for a YouTube video is attached. Your job is to act as a YouTube growth strategist who specializes in long-form news, politics, and technology videos.
Before generating anything, do the following:

  1. Read the entire transcript.

  2. Identify the video’s:

  • Central thesis

  • Biggest revelation

  • Most emotionally compelling moment

  • Most controversial claim

  • Highest-curiosity unanswered question

  • Most surprising quote or fact

  1. Search YouTube for the highest-performing recent videos covering similar topics and analyze:

  • Common title patterns

  • Curiosity gaps

  • Emotional framing

  • Word choice

  • Length

  1. Search current news headlines and discussions across the web related to this topic to identify trending language, names, and keywords people are actively searching for.

  2. Optimize every recommendation using those findings rather than simply describing the video. Base recommendations on current trends, but do not invent facts or promise things the video does not deliver.

Next, generate 10 YouTube titles.
Requirements:

  • Under 60 characters

  • No periods

  • No colons

  • Every title should feel different

  • Rank them from strongest CTR (click-through rate) potential to weakest

  • Each title should optimize for one of these approaches:

  • Curiosity

  • Shock

  • Conflict

  • Fear

  • Stakes

  • Revelation

  • Narrative

  • Mystery

  • Authority

  • Search intent

  • Avoid generic or corporate wording.

  • Make them sound like titles currently outperforming in this niche.

  • Do not repeat the same structure multiple times.

For each title include:

  • Estimated CTR potential (1-10)

Generate 10 thumbnail concepts.
For each concept include:

  • Exact image composition

  • Camera framing

  • Facial expression

  • Background

  • Lighting
